records.name: Diverge, then converge

origin.author: J. P. Guilford; Alex Osborn
origin.work: The Nature of Human Intelligence; Applied Imagination
origin.note: Guilford coined divergent/convergent production; Osborn's deferred-judgment rule.

records.summary: Generate first with judgment switched off, evaluate afterwards in a separate pass. Mixing the two kills weak-but-promising ideas before they can be improved.
records.key_question: Am I judging ideas while I am still supposed to be producing them?
records.card: No judging for the next ten ideas. Write the bad ones too.
use_when: I keep shooting down my own ideas
we argue about ideas as soon as they are said
I want a big list first and a shortlist later
every idea gets criticised in the room
records.produces: two separated passes: an unjudged idea list, then a shortlist
records.failure_mode: The judging pass never happens and the unfiltered list is treated as the result.

records.name: Idea quota

origin.author: Dean Keith Simonton
origin.work: Creativity in Science; equal-odds rule papers

records.summary: Set a number before starting and do not stop short of it. Hit rates per idea are roughly constant, so more attempts produce more good ones; the best ideas tend to arrive late in a run.
records.key_question: How many ideas will I produce before I am allowed to stop?
records.evidence_note: Equal-odds rule: quality of output tracks quantity across careers (Simonton). Late-arriving best ideas: serial order effect (e.g. Beaty & Silvia 2012). Effect sizes vary by task.
records.card: Twenty ideas. The good ones usually start after number twelve.
use_when: I run out of ideas after five
give me a lot of ideas
I stop at the first decent idea
how many ideas should I come up with
records.produces: a numbered idea list that reached its target count
records.failure_mode: Padding the list with near-duplicates to hit the number.

records.name: Brainwriting
records.summary: Each person writes ideas silently, then passes them on for others to build on. Avoids the production blocking and conformity that make verbal group brainstorming underperform.
records.key_question: Are people generating alone before the loudest voice sets the direction?
records.evidence_note: Nominal groups outproduce interactive groups (Diehl & Stroebe 1987, robust across replications); brainwriting variants close most of the gap.
records.card: Everyone writes three ideas in five minutes. No talking. Then swap.
use_when: our brainstorms get dominated by two people
ideas for a team workshop
quiet people never speak up
we need more ideas from the whole group
steps: State the challenge in one sentence and give everyone paper or a shared document.
Each person writes three ideas silently in a few minutes.
Pass the sheets on; each person adds to or builds on the ideas in front of them.
Repeat until every sheet has passed through every hand.
Collect all ideas onto one wall and cluster them before any discussion.
records.produces: a pooled idea wall from every participant, written independently
records.failure_mode: Skipping the silent round and falling back to open discussion.

records.name: SCAMPER
records.summary: Seven transformations applied to something that already exists: substitute, combine, adapt, modify, put to another use, eliminate, reverse. Turns 'improve this' into seven concrete prompts.
records.key_question: Which of the seven moves have I not tried on this yet?
records.card: Pick one letter: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to other use, Eliminate, Reverse.
use_when: how can I improve this product
make this existing thing better
I have something that works but feels stale
variations on an existing service
steps: Name the existing thing and what it does today.
Take each of the seven moves in turn: substitute, combine, adapt, modify, put to another use, eliminate, reverse.
Write at least two quick ideas for each move, even weak ones.
Mark the moves that produced nothing and leave them for a later round.
Cluster the ideas and carry the strongest clusters forward.
records.produces: a list of variations grouped by move, at least two per move
records.failure_mode: Running only the first two or three moves and stopping.

records.name: Morphological box

origin.author: Fritz Zwicky
origin.work: Discovery, Invention, Research through the Morphological Approach

records.summary: List the independent dimensions of a solution, list options on each, then combine one option per dimension. Makes the whole design space visible and surfaces combinations nobody would have proposed.
records.key_question: What are the dimensions, and which combination has nobody tried?
records.card: Three columns, five options each. Pick a combination at random and defend it.
use_when: I need a new product concept
there are several independent choices in this design
systematically explore all the combinations
what hasn't been tried
steps: List the independent dimensions of the solution (for example who, where, how, when, price).
Under each dimension write every option you can think of.
Make sure dimensions are independent of each other; merge any that are not.
Choose one option per dimension to form a concept; do this many times, including odd combinations.
Select the combinations that nobody around you would have proposed.
records.produces: a grid of dimensions and options plus a list of unusual combinations
records.failure_mode: Dimensions that depend on each other, which produces impossible combinations.

records.name: Resolve the contradiction
records.summary: State the problem as a contradiction: improving X worsens Y. Then look for a principle that removes the trade-off (separate in time, in space, by condition, by scale) instead of compromising between the two.
records.key_question: What gets worse when this gets better, and how could both improve?
records.card: Name the trade-off. Now separate it in time, space or scale.
use_when: we can't have both quality and speed
improving one thing breaks another
stuck in a trade-off
I keep compromising between two goals
steps: Write the contradiction as: improving A makes B worse.
Ask whether A and B conflict at all times or only under some conditions.
Try the four separations: in time, in space, by condition, by scale.
Check a list of inventive principles for ones that fit your separation.
Write each candidate as a concrete change, not a compromise.
records.produces: a statement of the contradiction and candidate separations that remove it
records.failure_mode: Settling for a midpoint compromise and calling it a resolution.

records.name: Inside-the-box templates
records.summary: Five moves applied to the existing components of a product or process: subtract an essential part, divide it, multiply a part with a change, give one part an extra job, link two variables that were independent.
records.key_question: What happens if I remove the part that seems essential?
records.evidence_note: Template-based ideation outperformed free ideation in expert-rated originality (Goldenberg, Mazursky & Solomon, Science 1999). Lab study; transfer to field settings less tested.
records.card: Remove the component everyone thinks is essential. What could it still do?
use_when: improve a mature product with what we already have
ideas without adding cost
a new use for our existing parts
innovate within the current resources
steps: List the components of the product or process and the attributes that matter.
Apply subtraction: remove an essential part and ask what the product becomes.
Apply division, multiplication, task unification and attribute dependency to the components.
Write one concrete idea per template application.
Keep ideas that use only things already in the system.
records.produces: an idea list generated from five template moves on existing components
records.failure_mode: Treating every template as mandatory and forcing ideas that do not fit.

records.name: Subtraction

origin.author: Gabrielle Adams, Benjamin Converse, Andrew Hales, Leidy Klotz

records.summary: People default to adding when they improve something. Explicitly ask what to remove. The subtractive option is often cheaper and better, and is missed unless prompted.
records.key_question: What could I take away instead of adding?
records.evidence_note: Eight experiments, Nature 2021: participants overlooked subtractive solutions unless cued. Robust within the paradigm; applied effect sizes unknown.
records.card: Solve it only by removing things.
use_when: this process has too many steps
we keep adding features
simplify this
what can we remove
records.produces: a list of removable parts with the effect of removing each
records.failure_mode: Removing something that carried a real function that nobody wrote down.

records.name: Attribute listing
records.summary: Break the thing into its attributes (material, shape, price, user, timing) and change one attribute at a time. A disciplined way to find improvements in a mature product.
records.key_question: Which single attribute have I never questioned?
records.card: List eight attributes. Change the most taken-for-granted one.
use_when: improve a product feature by feature
a mature product needs fresh ideas
systematic improvement ideas
which part of this could change
steps: Pick the thing and list its attributes: parts, materials, shape, price, user, place, timing.
Take one attribute at a time and write alternatives for it.
Pair a changed attribute with the others to see what it implies.
Highlight changes the customer would notice.
Cluster and shortlist.
records.produces: an attribute table with alternatives per attribute
records.failure_mode: Listing only physical attributes and ignoring the user, place and timing.

records.name: Assumption reversal
records.summary: List the assumptions a domain takes for granted, flip each one into its opposite, then ask how the reversed version could work.
records.key_question: What does everyone here assume, and what if the opposite were true?
records.card: Write the rule of this industry. Now build a business on its opposite.
use_when: everyone does it this way
challenge how we usually do this
I want a contrarian angle
what if the opposite were true
steps: List ten or more assumptions that people in this domain take for granted.
Rewrite each assumption as its opposite.
For each reversed statement, ask how it could work and who would benefit.
Pick the two most surprising reversals and develop each into an idea.
Flag which assumptions looked like real constraints for later checking.
records.produces: a list of assumptions, their reversals and developed ideas from the best two
records.failure_mode: Reversing the obvious assumptions and never finding the hidden ones.

records.name: Provocation (PO)
records.summary: State something deliberately false or impossible, then use it as a stepping stone: extract a principle from it, move to a workable idea. Judging the provocation itself is the mistake.
records.key_question: If this absurd statement were true, what useful principle would it point to?
records.card: Say something impossible about the problem. Then mine it.
use_when: I need a breakthrough, not an improvement
we are in a rut
something crazy to start from
think laterally about this
steps: Write a deliberately false or impossible statement about the topic, such as 'the shop has no customers'.
Do not judge it; ask what would follow if it were true.
Extract a principle or a moment of value from the provocation.
Move from the principle to a workable idea.
Write the idea down without referring to the provocation.
records.produces: a provocation, the principle drawn from it and a workable idea built on that principle
records.failure_mode: Dismissing the provocation as silly instead of using it as a stepping stone.

records.name: Random entry
records.summary: Pick an unrelated word or object at random and force connections between it and the problem. Breaks the well-worn association paths the mind returns to.
records.key_question: What does this random thing have to do with my problem?
records.card: Draw a random noun. Connect it to the problem three different ways.
use_when: I am stuck on the same few ideas
I need names or concepts that are different
give me something unexpected
break my usual train of thought
steps: Choose a random word from a list, a book or a prompt generator, not one related to the topic.
Write down ten attributes, associations and uses of that word.
Force a connection between each and the problem.
Capture every idea, then trim.
Draw a second random word if the first yields nothing.
records.produces: a list of forced-connection ideas from one or two random words
records.failure_mode: Rejecting the random word as irrelevant instead of forcing connections.

records.name: Bisociation
records.summary: Creative insight as the collision of two frames of reference that do not normally meet. Deliberately pair the problem with an unrelated domain and look for the point of contact.
records.key_question: Which unrelated field, collided with this one, produces something new?
records.card: Pick a field with no connection to yours. Where do the two meet?
use_when: what two worlds could meet here
combine two unrelated fields
an unexpected pairing for a product
new concept from two domains
records.produces: a pairing of two unrelated domains and the new ideas at their intersection
records.failure_mode: Choosing two domains that are only superficially different and getting a pun, not an idea.

records.name: Make it strange

origin.author: William J. J. Gordon
origin.work: Synectics: The Development of Creative Capacity

records.summary: Use direct, personal and fantastic analogies to make the familiar strange: become the object, describe it as nature would solve it, imagine it without physical limits.
records.key_question: If I were the object itself, what would I want?
records.card: You are the product. Describe your day and what annoys you.
use_when: help me see this familiar thing differently
I'm too close to the problem
metaphors for my problem
what would it feel like to be the product
steps: Describe the problem and pick the object at its centre.
Direct analogy: how does something in nature or another field do this?
Personal analogy: imagine being the object; what do you feel, want, fear?
Fantasy analogy: if physics and budget did not matter, how would it work?
Return to the real problem and turn the best analogy into a concrete idea.
records.produces: three analogies and a concrete idea drawn from the strongest one
records.failure_mode: Staying in the metaphor and never translating it back into something buildable.

records.name: Who else solved this
records.summary: Abstract the problem to its structure, then search other fields for a solved problem with the same structure and transfer the solution.
records.key_question: Where has a problem with this exact structure already been solved?
records.evidence_note: Analogical transfer works when people are prompted to look for it; spontaneous transfer is rare (Gick & Holyoak 1980, 1983).
records.card: Strip your problem to one abstract sentence. Who solved that sentence?
use_when: has anyone solved something like this before
borrow a solution from another industry
we're not the first with this problem
look at how other fields handle this
steps: Restate the problem abstractly, stripped of domain words (for example 'moving many items quickly through a bottleneck').
Search other fields for a solved problem with the same structure.
List three or four candidate fields and how each solved it.
Map the parts of the solved case onto your case.
Write the transferred solution and note what does not map.
records.produces: an abstracted problem statement and two or three transferred solutions with the mapping noted
records.failure_mode: Transferring on surface similarity when the underlying structure differs.

records.name: Ask nature
records.summary: Restate the function needed (adhere, cool, filter, signal) and look for organisms that perform it. A specific form of analogical transfer with a large library.
records.key_question: How does nature perform this function?
records.card: Name the function. Which animal or plant already does it?
use_when: how would nature solve this
design inspired by biology
I need a way to cool, filter, stick or signal
ideas from animals and plants
steps: Restate the problem as a function: what must be done, not what object does it.
Ask which organisms need to do the same thing in their environment.
Study the strategy each organism uses and list its principles.
Translate each principle into a design idea for your context.
Note constraints that nature has that you do not, and the reverse.
records.produces: a function statement, candidate organisms and design ideas translated from their strategies
records.failure_mode: Copying the form of the organism and missing the principle behind it.

records.name: Adjacent possible

origin.author: Stuart Kauffman; Steven Johnson
origin.work: Investigations; Where Good Ideas Come From

records.summary: The ideas reachable now are one step from what already exists. Map what has just become possible (new tools, costs, behaviours) and look one step beyond it.
records.key_question: What became possible in the last two years that makes a new move one step away?
records.card: What is newly cheap, newly fast or newly allowed? Step once past it.
use_when: what is newly possible now
ideas that fit where technology is heading
a new product idea at the right time
what could we build with what just became cheap
records.produces: a list of recent enabling changes and the next-step ideas each one makes reachable
records.failure_mode: Listing trends without turning any of them into a specific next step.

records.name: Hold both opposites
records.summary: Conceive two opposite or contradictory ideas as true at the same time and build from the tension rather than choosing one.
records.key_question: What if both of the opposing options were true at once?
records.card: Write the two opposites. Design something where both hold.
use_when: two opposite options both seem right
I don't want to choose between these
how can it be both cheap and premium
reconcile two conflicting demands
records.produces: an idea in which two opposing statements are both treated as true
records.failure_mode: Collapsing into a compromise instead of holding both statements as fully true.

records.name: Dreamer, Realist, Critic

origin.author: Robert Dilts
origin.note: Dilts' model of how Walt Disney worked; avoid 'Disney' in the method name (trademark list).

records.summary: Three separate passes with three separate roles: the Dreamer imagines without limits, the Realist plans how it would actually work, the Critic finds the weak points. Never two roles at once.
records.key_question: Which of the three roles have I skipped or blended?
records.card: Five minutes as the Dreamer only. No 'but'.
use_when: how do I make a big idea realistic
my plan needs a dream phase and a reality check
work through an idea in stages
I keep mixing creativity and criticism
steps: Dreamer pass: write the ideal outcome with no limits and no judgment.
Take a physical or mental break to change role.
Realist pass: describe how each part could actually be done, with steps and resources.
Critic pass: list what could fail and what is missing.
Send the critic's notes back to the dreamer for a second round if needed.
records.produces: three separate written passes: the ideal, the plan and the weak points
records.failure_mode: Letting the critic speak during the dreamer pass, which empties the first pass.

records.name: Worst possible idea

origin.author: Unattributed (common facilitation practice)
origin.note: Origin unverified; attribute as common practice unless a source is found.

records.summary: Generate the worst ideas on purpose, then invert each one or find the grain of value inside it. Lowers the fear of looking foolish and exposes hidden criteria.
records.key_question: What would make this as bad as possible, and what does the reverse suggest?
records.card: Ten terrible ideas. Then flip each one.
use_when: the room is too serious
we are afraid of looking silly
ideas to avoid and what they teach
break a creative block by being terrible
steps: Ask for the worst possible ideas for the challenge and write them all.
Make the group compete on how terrible they can be.
Take each bad idea and write its opposite.
Look inside each bad idea for a grain of value or a hidden criterion.
Move the good inversions to the main idea list.
records.produces: a list of worst ideas, their inversions and the criteria they exposed
records.failure_mode: Treating it as a game only and never inverting the results.

records.name: Lotus blossom

origin.author: Yasuo Matsumura
origin.note: Attribution to Matsumura is common in creativity literature (e.g. Michalko); verify.

records.summary: A 3x3 grid with the challenge at the centre and eight themes around it; each theme becomes the centre of its own grid of eight ideas. Sixty-four ideas organised by theme.
records.key_question: Have I expanded every theme, or only the first two?
records.card: Centre: the challenge. Eight themes around it. Fill one full petal.
use_when: I need many ideas organised by theme
break a big topic into themes and expand each
a structured way to get 60 ideas
ideas for a complex topic
steps: Draw a 3x3 grid and write the challenge in the centre.
Fill the eight surrounding cells with themes or sub-topics.
Copy each theme to the centre of its own 3x3 grid.
Fill the eight cells around each theme with ideas.
Review the whole set and highlight the strongest ideas across themes.
records.produces: a lotus grid with eight themes and up to 64 ideas
records.failure_mode: Stopping after the first two or three themes.

records.name: Eliminate-Reduce-Raise-Create grid

origin.author: W. Chan Kim & Renée Mauborgne
origin.note: Do not use 'Blue Ocean' in the method name (trademark list).

records.summary: Four questions on the factors an industry competes on: which to eliminate, which to reduce below standard, which to raise above standard, which to create that nobody offers.
records.key_question: Which factor does everyone compete on that the customer does not value?
records.card: Pick one industry standard to eliminate and one never offered to create.
use_when: how do we stand out from competitors
differentiate our offer
a new angle on our market
we compete on the same things as everyone
steps: List the factors the industry competes on (price, speed, features, service, and so on).
Mark which factors to eliminate that the industry takes for granted.
Mark which to reduce well below the standard.
Mark which to raise well above the standard.
List new factors to create that nobody offers, then write the offer implied by the grid.
records.produces: a four-action grid (eliminate, reduce, raise, create) and the offer it implies
records.failure_mode: Raising everything and eliminating nothing, which only adds cost.

records.name: Add a constraint

origin.author: Patricia Stokes; Catrinel Haught-Tromp
origin.work: Creativity from Constraints; The Green Eggs and Ham hypothesis

records.summary: Impose an arbitrary limit (half the budget, no screens, one day, only existing staff) and solve within it. Constraints narrow the search and often push past the obvious.
records.key_question: What constraint would force me away from the obvious answer?
records.evidence_note: Haught-Tromp 2017 (Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts): constrained prompts produced more creative output. Single-lab evidence; treat as suggestive.
records.card: Solve it with zero budget. Then with a hundred times the budget.
use_when: too many options and no direction
what would I do with half the budget
force a fresh approach
ideas when time is short
steps: State the challenge and the normal way it is solved.
Pick an arbitrary constraint: half the budget, one day, no screens, only existing staff.
Generate ideas that satisfy the constraint.
Pick a second, different constraint and repeat.
Compare the ideas and keep those that survive without the constraint.
records.produces: idea sets from two or more imposed constraints
records.failure_mode: Choosing a constraint so mild that it changes nothing.

records.name: Ten times, not ten percent
records.summary: Aim for a tenfold improvement instead of a marginal one. Incremental targets invite incremental fixes; a tenfold target forces a different approach entirely.
records.key_question: What would have to be true to make this ten times better rather than ten percent?
records.card: Make it ten times better. What do you have to throw away?
use_when: a small improvement is not enough
what would make it ten times better
aim bigger on this goal
incremental changes are not working
records.produces: a restated goal at ten times the target and the changes it would force
records.failure_mode: Using a ten-times target on a decision where reliability matters more than ambition.

records.name: Crazy 8s

origin.author: Jake Knapp, John Zeratsky, Braden Kowitz
origin.note: From the Google Ventures sprint process; avoid trademarked process names.

records.summary: Eight distinct sketches or variations in eight minutes. The time pressure stops polishing and forces variety.
records.key_question: Can I produce eight different versions before I start refining one?
records.card: Eight variations in eight minutes. Stick figures allowed.
use_when: I need many different versions fast
sketch ideas for a screen or layout
give me variations quickly
get unstuck on the first idea
steps: Fold a sheet into eight panels or open eight blank boxes.
Set a timer for eight minutes.
Sketch or describe a different version in each panel, about one minute each.
Do not refine; move on when the minute ends.
Pin the sheets up and mark the two or three most promising.
records.produces: eight distinct rough versions of one idea
records.failure_mode: Polishing the first panel instead of moving on.

records.name: Mind map
records.summary: Put the challenge at the centre and branch outward by association, one word per branch. Useful to map a space quickly before choosing where to dig.
records.key_question: Which branch did I abandon too early?
records.card: Centre word. Five branches. Push the strangest branch three levels deeper.
use_when: map out everything about this topic
I'm not sure where to dig yet
organise my scattered thoughts into branches
see the whole space of options
steps: Write the topic in the centre.
Draw main branches for the major themes, one word each.
Add sub-branches by association, quickly and without editing.
Circle links between branches that touch.
Pick two or three branches to take into a deeper method.
records.produces: a one-page map of branches and cross-links with chosen areas to explore
records.failure_mode: Drawing a tidy outline instead of following associations, which adds no new connections.

records.name: Borrowed eyes

origin.author: Rick Griggs (role storming)
origin.note: Role-storming attribution to Griggs is commonly cited; verify.

records.summary: Generate ideas as a specific other person or role would: a competitor, a child, a regulator, a famous designer, your harshest customer. Each persona unlocks ideas you would self-censor.
records.key_question: How would someone with completely different incentives attack this?
records.card: You are your fiercest competitor. How do you beat you?
use_when: how would a competitor see this
ideas from the customer's point of view
I'm stuck in my own way of seeing it
what would a ten-year-old do
steps: List five or six distinct roles: a competitor, a child, a regulator, an expert from another field, a harsh critic.
Take one role at a time and write down their goals and fears.
Generate ideas the way that person would attack the problem.
Switch role after a few minutes.
Collect all ideas and note which ones came only from a role you rarely take.
records.produces: idea lists written in several distinct personas
records.failure_mode: Using roles that think the way you do, which repeats your own ideas.

records.name: Yes, and
records.summary: Accept the previous idea and build on it before adding a new one. Keeps a chain of ideas growing instead of resetting with each contribution.
records.key_question: Did I build on the last idea or replace it?
records.card: Take the last idea. Say 'yes, and' three times in a row.
use_when: ideas keep dying in the meeting
build on what the last person said
grow one idea instead of replacing it
improv-style ideation
records.produces: a chain of developed ideas where each builds on the previous one
records.failure_mode: Saying yes-and to everything and never moving to selection.

records.name: Incubate

origin.author: James Webb Young; Ut Na Sio & Thomas Ormerod
origin.work: A Technique for Producing Ideas; Does incubation enhance problem solving? (meta-analysis)

records.summary: Load the problem fully, then step away to unrelated activity before returning. Breaks fixation on the first approach.
records.key_question: Have I loaded the problem fully, and then actually stepped away from it?
records.evidence_note: Sio & Ormerod 2009 meta-analysis: positive incubation effect, larger for divergent tasks. Mechanism disputed.
records.card: Write everything you know. Walk away. Come back tomorrow with fresh eyes.
use_when: I've been staring at this for hours
I need a break but want to solve it
sleep on it
let it simmer
records.produces: a written problem load, a scheduled break and a review of what changed on return
records.failure_mode: Taking the break without loading the problem first, so nothing incubates.

records.name: Oblique prompts

origin.author: Panta Rhei prompt deck (inspired by Brian Eno & Peter Schmidt)
origin.note: Ship only original prompts. Oblique Strategies text is copyrighted and on the trademark list as a name.

records.summary: A deck of short, indirect instructions drawn at random when stuck. Ships with its own original prompts; the Eno–Schmidt cards are not reproduced.
records.key_question: What does a sideways instruction make me try that a direct one would not?
records.card: Draw an oblique prompt and obey it literally for five minutes.
use_when: I'm completely stuck
we've tried everything
give me a sideways instruction
a nudge to break a creative block
steps: State the challenge and the current approach in one line.
Draw a prompt from the deck without choosing.
Follow the instruction literally for a few minutes and note what it changes.
If it fits nothing, draw again once.
Keep whatever the prompt changed in your approach.
records.produces: a changed approach to the challenge, recorded after following one or two prompts
records.failure_mode: Redrawing until the prompt is comfortable, which defeats the point.

records.name: Intersection
records.summary: Ideas cluster where fields, cultures and disciplines intersect. Bring in a person or a body of knowledge from outside the domain on purpose.
records.key_question: Who from a completely different field should look at this?
records.card: Invite a chef, a pilot and a nurse. What would each change?
use_when: who from another field could help
ideas where two disciplines meet
our group thinks alike
bring in outside knowledge
records.produces: a list of outside fields or people to consult and the questions to ask them
records.failure_mode: Inviting outsiders and then filtering their input through insider assumptions.
